items.text: google.protobuf.Any is not used anywhere in the current codebase — only google.protobuf.Struct appears (in ToolCallEventData.input and ErrorEventData.details). Round 2 settled on Any for the event payload, which is still the right choice (type URL-based runtime type checking is better than Struct for typed event payloads), but implementation will need to add the Any import and establish the pattern for the first time. The buf.yaml already depends on google/protobuf so no config changes needed.

Discovery callsites follow a wrapper pattern: scenarios define functions like resolveAgentManagerBaseURL() or locateIssueTrackerAPIPort() that call discovery.ResolveScenarioURL/Port. Event emission should be injected as a decorator around the Resolver struct (e.g., an EmittingResolver that wraps CommandRunner), not at each callsite. This keeps emission centralized and automatic — any scenario using the discovery package gets event emission for free.

Policy rules table schema (for all three policy kinds stored together):

CREATE TABLE policy_rules (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  kind TEXT NOT NULL CHECK(kind IN ('access','rate_limit','circuit_breaker')),
  source_pattern TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '*',
  target_pattern TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '*',
  action_pattern TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '*',
  priority INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  rule_data TEXT NOT NULL,
  enabled INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%f','now')),
  updated_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%f','now'))
);

The 'rule_data' column holds JSON-serialized typed rule payload (AccessRule, RateLimit, or CircuitBreaker proto serialized to JSON). Pattern columns use glob syntax for most-specific-wins matching. Priority is the specificity score (higher = more specific = wins).

items.context: No rate limiting exists in the codebase. The policy model includes rate limiting as a typed proto rule, but the enforcement algorithm is unspecified. Rate limits need to be evaluated at both sender-side (discovery cache) and receiver-side (middleware) with consistent semantics. The algorithm must be efficient for high-frequency evaluation and work with the dual-end cache model.

options.label: Token bucket: fixed capacity refilled at a steady rate
options.rationale: Allows bursts up to bucket capacity while enforcing average rate. Simple state (tokens remaining + last refill time). Industry standard for API rate limiting (used by AWS, Stripe). Easy to cache — just two numbers per rule. Slightly more complex than fixed window but avoids the boundary spike problem.

options.label: Sliding window log: track timestamps of recent requests, count within window
options.rationale: Most accurate — no boundary effects. But requires storing every request timestamp within the window, which is memory-intensive at high volume. Better suited for low-traffic precision scenarios.

options.label: Fixed window counter: count requests per time interval, reset at interval boundary
options.rationale: Simplest implementation — one counter per window. But has the well-known boundary spike problem: 2x allowed rate is possible at window edges. Less suitable for scenarios with bursty traffic.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Specify your own rate limiting algorithm

items.context: Both sender and receiver maintain local policy caches loaded at startup and updated via SSE. When a policy rule changes on the vrooli-events server, the caches need to stay synchronized. The invalidation strategy affects consistency guarantees, SSE bandwidth, and client complexity.

options.label: Full snapshot push: on any rule change, push the entire policy ruleset via SSE
options.rationale: Simplest client logic — replace entire cache atomically. No partial state issues. But bandwidth-heavy if the ruleset grows large. Acceptable for early stage when rule count is low (dozens, not thousands).

options.label: Incremental delta: push only changed/added/removed rules with version numbers
options.rationale: Bandwidth-efficient for large rulesets. But clients must handle partial updates, version conflicts, and gap detection (what if they missed a delta?). More complex but scales better.

options.label: Version-checked pull: SSE notifies of version bump, clients pull full snapshot from HTTP endpoint
options.rationale: SSE stays lightweight (just version notifications). Clients fetch at their own pace. Tolerant of missed SSE messages. But adds HTTP round-trip latency to policy updates and requires a separate endpoint.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Specify your own cache invalidation strategy

items.topic: Specificity scoring for access control rules
items.context: Round 2 settled on most-specific-wins for access control. The scoring algorithm determines which rule wins when multiple match. Patterns in source_pattern, target_pattern, and action_pattern use glob syntax. The score must be deterministic, explainable, and fast to compute (evaluated on every event).

options.label: Segment-count scoring: exact=3pts, prefix-glob=2pts, wildcard=1pt, sum across source+target+action
options.rationale: Simple and fast — one pass per rule. Maximum score is 9 (all exact). Ties broken by earliest creation. Easy to explain to policy authors: more specific patterns = higher score.

options.label: Longest-prefix scoring: count non-wildcard characters in each pattern, sum for total specificity
options.rationale: Finer granularity — 'swarm-manager.backlog.*' beats 'swarm-*'. But character counting is unintuitive for policy authors and expensive for complex patterns.

options.label: Explicit priority field: policy authors assign a numeric priority, highest wins
options.rationale: Maximum control but shifts complexity to authors. Risk of conflicting priorities. Requires governance process. Similar to iptables priority — powerful but error-prone.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Specify your own specificity scoring approach
